gabarito.reason:
This is a false positive. In ClientCerts.android.kt, tlsContext() passes SSLContext.init a custom MtlsKeyManager, an X509ExtendedKeyManager. It is built that way on purpose: on Android, a client certificate the user picked through android.security.KeyChain can only be reached through KeyChain.getPrivateKey and KeyChain.getCertificateChain. The private key is usually hardware-backed and can't be exported. It lives in the system KeyChain store, not in a KeyStore the app could hand to KeyManagerFactory.init. So a KeyManagerFactory-made KeyManager cannot present that key, and the platform docs show a custom X509KeyManager for exactly this KeyChain mTLS case.

The key manager also does work no factory can do. It picks a different alias for each gateway host, using the SNI host the socket factory saves in a ThreadLocal. It reads the key and chain at handshake time, so a renewed certificate or a revoked grant counts from the next handshake. When no alias matches the host it returns null, so gateways that don't use mTLS handshake exactly as before. It never chooses server aliases.

Trust is unaffected. The TrustManager comes from TrustManagerFactory.getDefaultAlgorithm() initialised with the system store, the protocol is "TLS", and SecureRandom is left at its default. No certificate or hostname check is weakened. The rule only flags where the KeyManager came from, which here is the right design and not a weakness. A PR that swapped in KeyManagerFactory would break client-certificate auth.

Second judge: This is an intentional custom-key-manager use, not a demonstrated TLS misuse. ClientCerts.android.kt passes MtlsKeyManager, an X509ExtendedKeyManager, to SSLContext.init; that API does not require managers to originate from KeyManagerFactory. The manager selects a gateway host's user-approved alias and obtains its private-key handle and certificate chain through Android KeyChain. ClientCertPicker.android.kt supplies the system picker, and SavedGateway persists only the alias. This implements the documented mTLS support for gateways behind ssl_verify_client, covering REST and /api/ws. Server trust still uses the default TrustManagerFactory, and OkHttp's hostname verification is unchanged. Replacing this with null managers or an ordinary factory's defaults would lose the selected client identity.

Delivery policy (v3, the same for every unit): a pull request, an issue and no action are all acceptable deliveries; judge each on its quality, not on whether it should have been sent. A pull request that changes the code only so that it satisfies the specification, without changing behaviour, is acceptable when it is correct, keeps every must_not_break constraint and does not present itself as a vulnerability fix; do not mark it down as unnecessary churn or because the finding is a false positive. Do not guess whether the runtime checker would still report the patched code; judge the code.
must_not_break: Client-certificate (mTLS) auth with KeyChain-held, non-exportable keys: KeyChain.getPrivateKey/getCertificateChain can't feed a KeyManagerFactory/KeyStore, so swapping MtlsKeyManager for a factory KeyManager would stop the app presenting the user's certificate

Choosing a certificate per host: MtlsKeyManager.chooseClientAlias looks up the alias for the captured SNI host (handshakeSniHost via SniCapturingSocketFactory), then the socket host, using clientCertAliasFor (pending Connect-screen picks first, then SavedGateway.clientCertAlias)
Gateways without a certificate must keep handshaking with no client certificate (a null alias means nothing is sent)

Key and chain are read at each handshake, not cached, so a renewed certificate or a revoked KeyChain grant counts from the next handshake; a null MtlsAppContext at startup or in host tests must mean no certificate rather than a crash
When ClientCertAliases.onChanged fires, a fresh SSLContext is swapped in (empty session cache) and the pool is evicted, so no session made with the old certificate is resumed
System-default trust from TrustManagerFactory plus OkHttp hostname checks; the same OkHttp engine serves the REST calls and the /api/ws upgrade
Existing tests in MtlsKeyManagerTest (androidHostTest) and ClientCertsTest
Preserve Android KeyChain selection and access to system-held private keys, including potentially non-exportable keys; do not require exporting keys or importing them into an app-managed keystore.

Preserve SavedGateway.clientCertAlias in gateways.v1, legacy gateway migration, older records with no alias, and certificate retention across sign-in. Keep storing aliases rather than private-key material.

Preserve live host-specific alias selection from pending Connect-screen picks and saved gateways, including host normalization, hostname capture despite OkHttp connecting by IP, and no arbitrary fallback to another host's certificate. Hostless socket creation must clear stale captured host information.

Preserve client authentication for connection probes, sign-in, gateway REST requests, and the /api/ws upgrade against servers requiring client certificates. Gateways without a selected certificate must continue to work without one.

Preserve certificate-change handling: immediately replace the TLS context to discard resumable sessions and evict idle pooled connections off the main thread. Existing active calls and WebSockets retain their current identity until closed.

Preserve lazy KeyChain access on handshake threads, safe engine construction before the application context exists, and fresh lookups that observe certificate renewal or revoked access on subsequent handshakes.
Preserve default server certificate validation and hostname verification, Android API 26 support, and the desktop implementation's operation without a system client-certificate picker.
